This paper focuses on the investigation of structural, electronic, and magnetic properties for GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We calculated the lattice parameters, bulk modulus, band structures, and magnetic properties for these materials. The results show that GdSn3 and CmSn3 have a hexagonal Ni2In-type structure and exhibit semimetallic characteristics with magnetic properties. The density of states at the Fermi level for these materials is very low in the nonmagnetic state, confirming their stability in a magnetic state. For the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, the calculated parameters match experimental measured values for x = 1, and the materials maintain a stable magnetic state across various compositions. The indirect magnetic gap can be found in the projected density of states for all calculated layers of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series.

Theoretical models predicting the existence of extra baryons and mesons beyond the standard $SU(3)$ spectrum also anticipate the creation of additional particles within meson nonet, decuplet, and antidecuplet groups at the LHC. To facilitate the identification of these particles, this study employs the parameters of leading-order QCD and IR-evolution kernels to calculate their expected properties, including distribution functions, fragmentation functions, and pole masses. A threshold resummation in the pole mass case accounts for the effects of high-logarithm resummation. Additionally, the study considers the role of multiple gluon exchanges within the color-coherence framework and mass hierarchies, which influence the creation of heavy quark-antiquark pairs. Theoretical predictions for the production of heavy-flavored mesons at the LHC, specifically for the 7 and 8 TeV energy scales, are provided, along with the relevant NNLO cross-section calculations for benchmark processes. The study offers the necessary tools for experimentalists to connect theoretical predictions to observed phenomena and make predictions for unobserved particles within meson nonet, decuplet, and antidecuplet groups based on the non-observation limits of their production at the LHC.

The foundation theorem is a significant tool in the theory of Coxeter groups, enabling the reduction of any Coxeter system to a fundamental system represented by a single irreducible root. However, the foundational property is lost under reflections within the B-type Coxeter groups due to the presence of dihedral groups of order greater than 4. This paper proves that the foundation theorem remains viable for B-type Coxeter groups by identifying a specific reflection sequence that yields a fundamental root, thereby bypassing the limitation of a single consecutive reflection path.

Utilizing weak lensing, we calculated the convergence field at a specific redshift, $z=0.45$, and found that it significantly affects the observed brightness of Type Ia Supernovae at that redshift. This effect is noticeable even when analyzing a large dataset like the Pantheon collection. We discovered that after accounting for the intrinsic brightness variations of these supernovae, the impact of weak lensing on their observed magnitude is $0.08\sigma$, which is comparable to the influence of supernovae light curve shape. This finding holds when we consider how gravitational field distorts the light curve can affect this estimation. We found a small correlation between the shear field and the intrinsic brightness of these supernovae, but when we factored in this effect, the amplification due to weak lensing is still $0.06\sigma$. This result provides the most precise measurement of this effect so far, and it has implications for cosmological analyses involving Type Ia Supernovae, particularly when combining them with other probes to study the history of the expansion rate of the universe.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included. 

The concluding chapter covers the pathwise approach.

In this analysis, a novel type of mode converter, known as a T hub, is theoretically described for dielectric material systems. This T hub structure is capable of efficiently converting circularly polarized light into linearly polarized light, with a specific polarization angle, and vice versa. Our calculations demonstrate that a silicon-on-silicon oxide system can support this function with very low loss. Furthermore, simulations indicate that this T hub can effectively transfer circularly polarized light between two coaxial microcavity resonators, even when there is a significant overlap between the modes.

MRI scans utilize magnetic fields and radio waves to generate detailed images of the inside of the body. These images can be manipulated digitally through various mathematical transformations. This study investigates whether a machine learning algorithm can recognize manipulations made to an MRI image, specifically in the context of identifying tumors. With access to a comprehensive dataset containing MRI images of liver tumors, we developed and tested several manipulation techniques, including resizing, cropping, and distortions. These manipulations were applied at different spatial frequencies to certain regions of the scan. Our findings show that a neural network can accurately identify manipulated images 85% of the time. This suggests that tumors can be reliably detected even in low-quality MRI scans, based on analysis of the image's frequency content rather than its visual appearance.

The problem of determining whether a given set of numbers contains a non-degenerate Bernoulli number has been investigated by various researchers under different algebraic structures, specifically within the context of p-adic analysis. In our work, we excise the requirement for non-degeneracy and instead focus on a broader class of degenerate Bernoulli numbers, leveraging algebraic properties to identify them within a given set. Additionally, we establish connections between our approach and existing strategies, revealing that our method yields a stronger result in certain situations. Furthermore, we explore the application of our approach to a specific situation, identifying a non-degenerate solution within a set defined by a polynomial equation, X^2 + Y^3 = 1, over the integers.

The performance of solar spectral line analysis can be hampered by the numerous line collections used to derive physical parameters. Through a statistical approach, this study assesses how line choice affects the retrieval of best-fit parameters, including temperature, density, magnetic field strength, flow velocity, torsional wave mode, and beta values, in various regions of a magnetohydrodynamic model atmosphere. For a specific region, a specific line collection yielded a specific level of performance, with certain lines contributing the most to the error. However, when applying the same line collection to different regions, significant deviations in physical parameters were observed, with some lines again playing a significant role. On the other hand, a random line selection for least-squares deconvolution demonstrated a reduced scatter in physical parameters, with a specific velocity flow pattern emerging despite line variations. This method's ability to minimize the impact of line choice on physical parameters is thought to originate from its tendency to average out extreme line choices, thus enhancing the robustness of solar spectral line analysis.

In large-scale Wireless Sensor Networks, implementing efficient and adaptable data collection methods is crucial. One key technique utilized for this purpose is the ON-demand Gathering in Wireless Sensor Networks (OGMC) protocol, which creates hierarchical structures within the network by developing a robust and effective routing mechanism. However, the stability of these protocols relies heavily on the accuracy of forward and backward integrity estimations, which can be prone to distortions caused by outdated local and global scope indices. To address this challenge, a novel approach called Hierarchical Scope Sectoring (HISS) has been developed to bidirectionally evaluate integrity and create a stable framework for OGMC-based protocols. HISS utilizes a contextualized local scope sectoring method to enhance the precision of forward integrity estimations and a global scope sectoring approach for reverse evaluations. By integrating HISS with the 802.15.4 standard, simulations revealed a significant improvement in energy consumption, a 20% increase in delivery ratio, and a 10% decrease in network lifetime.

Context plays a significant role in object detection, yet the underlying assumption in pipeline methods is that objects are detected in isolation. To address this, we propose integrating contextual information into the detection pipeline using semantic features from intermediate features in a neural network. Specifically, we suggest extracting contextual information using two methods: first, by segmenting the context using the detected object as a mask; second, by employing self-supervision to refine the detected object region. Our approach is versatile and adaptable to various detection frameworks. With the proposed context assessment method, we achieved notable improvements in accuracy on the ADE20K semantic segmentation benchmark and COCO object detection benchmark, outperforming the baseline by 2.4% mIoU and 2.5% AP on average respectively.

The main objective here is to investigate an inhomogeneous Kirchhoff type elliptic equation where the nonlinearity, linked to the Sobolev embedding theorem, is treated with a singular Trudinger-Moser type condition. Leveraging a new concentration compactness approach, we are able to establish the existence and uniqueness of a positive solution for the given equation within a specific function space.

This paper examines the concentration behavior of functions of binary random variables whose dependencies are characterized by a specific set of weakly anti-correlated random variables. We demonstrate that if the underlying random variables satisfy particular inequality conditions related to their expectations and probabilities, then the probability of which the function deviates from its expected value by more than a certain amount is bounded by an expression involving those inequalities. The bound is shown to be achievable under certain correlation conditions. The results we obtain are relevant to the study of general anti-correlated random variables, enabling us to derive stronger inequalities for the concentration behavior of discrete entropy, total variation distance, and the probability of the minimum and maximum of a set of random variables.

Let k be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series R over the Witt vectors of k for its prime p. The main objective is to establish a Fontaine-Messing type theorem for crystalline (phi,N)-coherent modules under specific embeddings of R into a finite extension of the algebraic closure of the field of p-adic numbers.

This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine spin correlation observed in experiments, accounting for the interference term between the twist-2 contributions. The calculation reveals that the cosine spin correlation arises due to the difference between the helicity distributions of anti-quarks and the sum of the helicity distributions of quarks, in alignment with experimental data. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that the interference between the twist-2 and twist-3 contributions can be negligible for the cosine spin correlation when the hadron pairs' invariant mass is substantial.

In quantum gravity, the concept of time remains abstract and needs to be defined through physical processes. A notable approach establishes a link between spatial volumes in quantum gravity and the Fock space, effectively treating physical systems as states within this space. Building upon this framework, we derive a method to relate the Fock space to de Sitter space, focusing on the thermodynamic properties of spatial volumes in quantum gravity. Specifically, we show that the partition function for these volumes is equivalent to the number density of Weyl-like modes in the de Sitter space, and that the corresponding entropy is proportional to the de Sitter horizon area. Leveraging this connection, we find that the Fock space sector of quantum gravity is characterized by a non-zero chemical potential, which reflects the intrinsic chemistry of spatial volumes in quantum gravity. The chemical potential is found to be linked to the de Sitter mass parameter and determines the number of Weyl-like modes within the Fock space. The relationship between the Fock space and de Sitter space provides a physical interpretation of the chemical potential, suggesting that it arises from the interaction between quantum gravity volumes and the cosmological horizon.

We establish a clear and intuitive framework for understanding symplectic modifications. By drawing parallels with the concepts of blow-ups in complex geometry, we demonstrate that modifications maintain key properties, including preservation of symplectic form and structure. Leveraging this understanding, we can derive significant insights into the behavior of cohomology classes under modification procedures. Furthermore, our work enables the demonstration of a specific relationship between modified manifolds and their component submanifolds, thereby providing a comprehensive proof of a previously stated conjecture.

This paper introduces a new approach called Layered Diagram Embedding (LDE) for suggesting entities within the Yahoo! Knowledge Network, utilizing Wikipedia as a knowledge base. LDE takes a query as input and generates a list of entity recommendations ranked by relevance. To achieve this, LDE takes advantage of a unique representation of entities as interconnected nodes, where relationships are hierarchically organized and easily navigable. An innovative feature of LDE is its ability to leverage the structural composition of entities, combining the properties of nodes to enhance the ranking of recommended entities. Through Wikipedia, LDE utilizes Inter-Linked Merge Operations to effectively incorporate structural information into the entity ranking task. Our experiments demonstrate that LDE surpasses existing methods in entity suggestion benchmarks and provides a superior entity ranking module for the Wikipedia-based entity suggestion task.

The life of a transplant recipient who has received a kidney from a donor is not always easy. To make the most of their transplant, recipients must adhere to a strict pre-emptive immunosuppression regimen for the rest of their life. This study aims to identify factors that influence the level of disruption caused by incompatible donors on a recipient's life. Using a mixed-methods design, we gathered quantitative and qualitative data from 106 transplant recipients in the US. Our findings reveal that recipients who received kidneys from living donors experienced more life disruptions than those who received kidneys from deceased donors. Specifically, they had a higher risk of developing post-transplant complications, struggling with medication adherence, missing work or school, and managing stress related to the transplant. Our research can be used to develop programs that provide tailored support to help recipients from incompatible donors readjust to their new life.

This study seeks to clarify the implicit connections between explicit connections in graph theory and the implicit connections in information theory, specifically within the Wyner-Ziv source coding theorem. We establish an explicit formula for the rate distortion function using the shortest path distance, which may lead to further understanding of how rate and distortion are interconnected. To verify the accuracy of this formula, we also derive the rate distortion function for two specific scenarios using both implicit and explicit approaches.

Recent studies utilizing neural language models (NLMs) have reported improvements in predicting text polarity, leveraging the Large Language Model Archive (LLAMA) dataset as a testing ground. This research employs the LLAMA dataset to assess the capability of word representations to distinguish between financial text's semantic polarity. Our analysis showcases the effectiveness of neural network-based polarity classification and highlights the limitations of word representations. Specifically, our findings indicate that the richness of these representations is insufficient to grasp the underlying semantic polarity. This insight suggests the necessity for embeddings that incorporate polarity information in their context.

This article proposes a novel end-to-end system architecture that considers integrated information and power transfer in an OFDM-based communication system. The model enables the analysis of energy transfer via a real impedance load and information transfer via an arbitrary impedance load. To facilitate positive energy transfer, an impedance matching condition specific to the system is derived. A dimensionless variable representing the degree of freedom in the integrated system is defined and maximized to derive the optimal impedance loads for energy and information transfer, respectively. Furthermore, the optimal variable loads can be implemented using varactor-based impedance tuning technologies. The proposed system architecture is demonstrated to provide a gain of over two times the square root of the number of antennas and carriers compared to separate systems. The theoretical gain is verified through numerical simulations and practical demonstrations.

This research introduces a hybrid level-set/embedded boundary method to solve problems involving the movement of fluids in the presence of solids forming through precipitation.
The approach combines the level-set technique for handling curved boundaries with the embedded boundary method to model surfaces that form naturally, and has been successfully tested on several scenarios, including the movement of a melting crystal, boundary layer stability, and the formation of convection patterns in a solidifying alloy.

In the realm of linguistic inquiry, as with the study of quantum systems, superposition holds significant meaning. This concept, central to our proposed theoretical framework known as Quantum Linguistics, is particularly relevant when analyzing how the structure of sentences conveys different pragmatic implications. Our model builds upon the foundation established by Jakobek and Halter, incorporating a novel twist that utilizes a single unary operator to achieve the same unifying effects as classical sentential connectives, specifically through the application of a controlled NOT gate. By doing so, we demonstrate that the choice of sentence type (e.g., affirmative, negative, or interrogative) serves as a kind of superposition, influencing the expression of multiple pragmatic implications simultaneously. Furthermore, this twist enables us to explore the metaphysical theory of Type Physicalism, the idea that the fundamental physical properties of linguistic expressions correspond to category-specific quantum states.

We investigate a private-aggregate single-shot game among $n$ self-interested agents, where agents' valuation functions are characterized by unknown mixed strategies, and a dominant equilibrium exists characterized by a rationalizable mixed strategy profile. We pin down essentially optimal communication requirements for two significant cases: when the aggregate payoff function is known, or when agents can query the functional form of the aggregate payoff, both under various levels of privacy constraints. When the aggregate payoff is known, just one bit of communication is sufficient; we show that this result deteriorates to $n^2$ bits without knowledge of the functional form. When the functional form is accessible, we find a suitable path from an exploratory start to exact recovery of the equilibrium, involving an information gathering path of length $O(n\log n)$. We also establish that this result is nearly optimal. Our study offers a comprehensive examination of the interplay between two critical components in our setting: the complexity of the game (captured by the number of players) and the ambiguity of the valuation functions (captored by the self-interested nature of the agents).

Researchers studying graph theory who rewire their edges randomly upon infection can provide valuable insights that apply to various real-world scenarios. This research examines how SIS dynamics and new infection patterns affect the behavior of these rewiring rules on both fixed and dynamic graphs. It's found that on a random graph model, specific infection patterns cause the basic reproduction number to drop below one, stopping the spread of the epidemic, while the same reduction in R0 doesn't halt the epidemic on a configuration model. Additionally, the research demonstrates that certain graph properties influence the impact of the epidemic on the rewiring process, and it identifies distinct phases in the dynamics of a dynamic graph model that resemble epidemic-driven percolation. This research provides a foundation for further exploration of dynamic processes on complex networks.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally isometric to a non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator and a non-zero eigen value.

The xFitter working group within the HIC collaboration developed the xFitter framework, which provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for explaining data related to structure functions and form factors. This framework, combining quantum chromodynamics with the Paschos-Ellis-Nanopoulos approach, allows for the calculation of observable quantities based on parton distribution functions. As a result, xFitter enables accurate adjustments to these parton distribution functions using observational data from experiments such as HERA, SCAN, COMPASS, and HFF, and incorporates established tools like LAPACK and ARPACK.

The effectiveness of variance-reduced experience replay (VRER) in combining multiple stochastic gradients was previously demonstrated. However, the underlying assumption of VRER that all minibatches are drawn independently and identically from the data distribution does not hold in practice, as minibatches are often over-revisited due to their similarity. To address this issue, a more realistic model is proposed that considers the non-uniform data distribution. Based on this model, a new variance-reduced algorithm called Variance-Reduced Experience Replay (VRER) with Overlap (VREO) is proposed to incorporate correlated minibatches, leading to a significant improvement in performance in challenging tasks such as navigation in complex environments and multi-task learning.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, an open-source Python library for computational condensed matter physics. It distinguishes itself from other languages through a unique syntax focused on defining quadratic Hamiltonians and their associated unitary transformations. Furthermore, libcommute incorporates a specialized diagonalization routine, leveraging the efficiency of the quark algebra library Quark and OpenMP for parallel processing. As a result, libcommute delivers exceptionally fast performance when dealing with multi-band, lattice-based systems, and the code is particularly well-suited for applications involving fractional quantum Hall states. The project also includes a range of examples highlighting its capabilities and a user-friendly interface via the pycommute frontend, which provides an interactive environment for the user to input parameters and observe the consequences on the system's properties.

Our calculation using the LDA+UDF method has provided a comprehensive understanding of the electronic architecture and phonon modes in the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ crystal. By examining the band structure and Fermi surface, we identified the primary locations and velocities of electrons around the Fermi surface, including the hole-like Fermi surface centered at the zone center and two electron-like Fermi surfaces situated at the M points of the zone edge. The calculated phonon modes reveal that the two primary modes in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{00.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ exhibit anomalous behavior, with decreasing frequencies as temperature drops below 300 K, due to the duration of time that electrons hold their position, lasting from a few femtoseconds to a few hundred femtoseconds, which significantly impacts the coupling between electrons and the vibrational motions of atoms. Moreover, the duration of time that electrons hold their position is found to be in the range of a few hundred femtoseconds, which is in line with the experimental findings of delayed gap opening and the formation of voids around the Fe atoms, as observed in the scanning transmission electron microscopy images.

A recent generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation achieves similar purposes to the classic one, notably enabling the decomposition of nonlinear Gaussian models into a solvable set of linear equations. A specific examination is made of whether the superbosonization equation can serve as a variant of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, considering both the mathematical properties and practical applications of the two methods. A key distinction found is that the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation involves a change of variable, in contrast to the bosonization process. A specific non-Markovian Gaussian model is then solved using both methods to compare their efficiency. The results show that the superbosonization equation can be a useful tool for bosonization, although the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation remains more versatile due to its variable transformation nature. The discussion is extended to nonlinear non-Gaussian models, providing the opportunity to address the issue of how the super-Fock space representation could be obtained for such models.

The study examines the signal-to-background ratio and observable distributions for the identification of top quark polarization in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions using the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. A set of observables specifically sensitive to the effects of QCD and electroweak interactions are considered, and their behavior is analyzed for events characterized by isolated same-sign dileptons and missing transverse momentum, resulting from the decay of top quarks produced through the t-channel process. Evaluations of the signal-to-background ratio, distribution tail weights, and polarization asymmetry metadynamics show the feasibility of distinguishing between left- and right-handed top quark polarization states via likelihood fitting.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the magnetic properties of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as a function of temperature and number of layers. Our $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR experiments revealed a distinctive shift in the LaAlO$_3$ layer's Knight shift as the temperature lowered, indicative of a nearby mobile charge carrier. Our findings demonstrate that the LaAlO$_3$ layer's spin susceptibility follows a similar temperature dependence as that of the LaNiO$_3$ layer, and is unaffected by the superlattice period. This demonstrates electronic coupling between the LaNiO$_3$ and LaAlO$_3$ layers across the interface.

Our proposed MultiTalk framework aims to create a diverse range of conversations 
by incorporating multiple independent conversation branches. This approach 
encompasses various conversation types such as multiple-round discussions, 
conversations with multiple participants, and conversations involving multiple 
topics. To achieve this, the framework utilizes multiple state machines to manage 
the conversation process, ensuring the states are consistent across all branches. 
To prevent the proliferation of hard-to-trace state transition errors, the team 
develops a proprietary dialogue manager tool that utilizes a graph-based error 
propagation method to pinpoint the source of the issue. Furthermore, the team 
integrates a proprietary neural semantic role labeling model, which was previously 
competitive with top-performing methods in baseline tests. The team showcases the 
framework's effectiveness through a demonstration of the model it developed, 
receiving the Outstanding Demonstration Award at the Conference.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, specifically one that utilizes multiple input and output antennas and a surface for signal reflection and phase shifting. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal inputs and a more realistic method of phase shifting. Through the application of the Max-Net decoder and a mathematical approach that represents the system's characteristics in an optimal way, we are able to define the maximum achievable capacity in terms of the system's characteristics and a specific function. Furthermore, we are able to analyze how increasing the number of correlated signal inputs affects this capacity, both positively and negatively, and find that the positive effect diminishes over time due to the presence of correlation. Additionally, we find that the use of a reflective surface for signal reinforcement and phase shifting can significantly increase the capacity in certain scenarios, including those with highly correlated signal inputs and a large number of such inputs.

We introduce a family of modified gravity models based on a conformally related metric, which alters the behavior of matter particles under specific scalar fields. This modification is distinct from $f(R)$ and $\mu$Sydney modifications. We develop an equation that governs the motion of N bodies in this context and demonstrate that this equation is suitable for numerical simulations. To facilitate the processing power required, we divide a spherical system into concentric shells and derive a method to accurately simulate the interaction within each shell while maintaining a reasonable level of precision. This allows us for the first time to simulate the behavior of a comprehensive N-body system in this modified gravity scenario. We validate our approach by comparing the outcomes to more sophisticated general N-body simulations conducted using the original altered gravity equations. These simplified simulations retain a high degree of precision at a significantly lower computational cost, making them exceptionally useful for furthering our understanding of this unique family of modified gravity models.

In the conformal field theory, the Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) is a fundamental process that is used to study conformally invariant random processes. Multiple independent SLEs can be used to investigate the interaction between conformally invariant random fields. Specifically, researchers are interested in the pairing of Gaussian free fields (GFFs) with SLEs, as this relationship enables the extraction of scaling dimensions for conformal field theories. This article focuses on pairing GFFs with multiple independent SLEs, where the GFF is defined as the conformal density of a random gas consisting of charged points. We establish the convergence of the pairings to the conformal field theories that correspond to minimal models, and this result is based on the careful analysis of the interactions between the GFF and the SLEs. By utilizing the conformal field theory on the Riemann surface with boundaries, we can extend our findings to a broader class of pairings, and we also investigate the relationship between the discrete and continuous time SLEs.

MediaWiki-based platforms like Wikipedia and WikiPathways have achieved notable success in collaborative research and knowledge sharing. To expand on this and provide a more comprehensive framework for cooperative projects, WorkingWiki has been developed. This extension enables media wikis to manage complex projects by integrating features such as task and annotation tools, customizable interfaces, and integrated discussion forums within a wiki environment. Through this framework, researchers can seamlessly integrate their expertise and contribute to common goals, facilitated by features such as user roles, version control, and collaborative editing.

This research investigates the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and a nearby wall in a perpendicular configuration, specifically examining how acoustic vibrations in the range of 0-50Hz affect this interaction. The study focuses on a specific area near the point where the jet meets the ground, using both numerical and experimental data to compare results. When acoustic vibrations aren't present, the data shows a good match between the two for temperature, CO2, and oxygen levels. However, introducing acoustic vibrations causes significant discrepancies, with the experiments showing a 10% increase in temperature variability, a 5% increase in CO2, and a 5% decrease in oxygen levels compared to the same data from the numerical model. Additionally, the experiments exhibit non-linear relationships between temperature and CO2, as well as a peak in oxygen levels at 20Hz. This discrepancy leads to the proposal of an active flame model, taking into account how acoustic vibrations impact the flame and surrounding gases. This model demonstrates a more accurate representation of the experimental data, including the non-linear relationship between temperature and CO2, and provides a framework for further research into the interaction between turbulent jet fires and structures in acoustically excited environments.

A novel technique called Time-Reversed Partial Correlation (TRPC) is the focus of this study, and it aims to identify unique patterns of activity in complex networks of interconnected neurons. When a group of neurons is functioning independently, their activity is uncorrelated with the behavior of other parts of the network. Conversely, if there is a significant statistical connection between the activity of some neurons and the rest of the network, it indicates those neurons are interdependent. To apply TRPC to real neural data, a simulation of spiking neural networks showed that it effectively pinpointed synchronized groups and chimera states. Chimera states are rare occurrences where some neurons fire consistently, while others fire randomly, and TRPC revealed these patterns without relying on fire rate calculations. Furthermore, TRPC successfully detected these complex patterns in networks much larger than previously thought possible with this method.

In certain spin systems and Ising models with long-range interactions, group of sites that share connections with each other exhibits unique and varied properties of order. Research has typically focused on systems where sites are equidistant from each other, but this study explores two-dimensional lattice fluids where sites located a variable distance from each other are capable of forming strong bonds. In this scenario, a range of different orders can emerge, with the specific configuration depending on the specific variables. This research aims to investigate the relationship between these variables and the emergence of order within these systems. A specific method has been developed to handle these complex variables, using a technique called the finite-cluster method that involves measuring the size of these ordered groups by looking at how they appear from outside. This measure has been found to correlate strongly with the probability of finding a group of sites in a state of order. The variable distance between sites can be thought of as a form of disorder within these systems, but interestingly this study has shown that the size of these ordered groups can be much larger than the distance between sites, displaying self-organization on a large scale. This research was conducted using Monte Carlo simulations on a variety of different lattice structures, but the findings were consistent across all of them.

Theoretical models predict that high-energy photons should flow isotropically from sources at the galactic center. Observations of these photons above $10^{19}$ eV, however, indicate an anisotropic distribution that resembles the structure of the galactic magnetic field. To better understand these findings, we use a numerical simulation to examine how the large-scale solar magnetic field affects the direction of extremely high-energy photons streaming from the galactic center. Our analysis takes into account the magnetic field's turbulence and considers particles with energies ranging from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ GeV. Our results indicate that the distribution of these photons relative to the direction of antiparallel magnetic fields can exhibit a significant anisotropy of up to 5.6 times its average value. This anisotropy is most pronounced when the angle between the photon direction and the local magnetic field is approximately 15 degrees. A specific observational signature that could validate our findings is the disparity in the photon flux measured head-on versus flux measured from the side, which may be as high as 2.5 times.

Nonlocal gravity represents a modification of general relativity where information travels at a finite speed, exceeding the speed of light, and this study explores its implications. We demonstrate that nonlocal gravity leads to the abandonment of the metric compatibility principle in gravity, resulting in the introduction of a new vector field that characterizes compatibility. This, in turn, enables the identification of essential tetrads that filter nonlocal effects from total metric information. Furthermore, we integrate nonlocal gravity within the metric formalism, introducing a new connection that distinguishes nonlocal from ambient (background) connections, and demonstrate that the nonlocal connection is compatible with the essential tetrads. This integration results in the derivation of nonlocal gravity equations that encompass both the gravitational and electromagnetic nonlocal effects, and their solutions indicate that nonlocal gravity may lead to the formation of stable, rotating relativistic stars with thicker crusts and faster cooling rates.

Distributed systems with replicated data require efficient handling of updates across multiple sites. The Eliminate-Win design, a novel approach for update validation, builds upon the foundation laid by previous theories. It operates under the assumption that an update is valid for a node if it is not present at a certain threshold ($k$) of neighboring sites. To validate an update, the design involves determining the number of nodes ($h$) where the update needs to be eliminated to avoid conflicts. A key aspect of the design is the elimination number, which represents the number of nodes needed to be eliminated to validate an update. It has been proven that the Eliminate-Win design is NP-hard to determine the validity of an update given the replication degree ($k$). A proposed algorithm, though not always optimal, can provide a valid update for a specific degree of replication ($k=3$). Furthermore, the design can be applied to data forms with cycles and has been validated through simulation with a focus on performance and consistency.

To facilitate the interpretation of genomic data, researchers and clinicians need access to detailed information about genomic elements such as promoters, exons, and chromatin marks, in addition to genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings. Unfortunately, current resources primarily offer aggregated data, lacking specific information about genomic components. To bridge this gap, we've created a database called GenomicProfile, which provides comprehensive information on genomic features and associated GWAS findings for various human traits. This database is built using a combination of publicly available resources and data from GWAS studies, and is designed to facilitate the exploration of genomic data related to these traits. By examining the genomic profile of a specific trait, users can gain insight into the functional components of the genome that are involved in the underlying biology of the trait. Furthermore, this profile can be used to identify potential targets for drugs or other therapies. GenomicProfile is an open-source platform that allows users to import their own GWAS data and create personalized genomic profiles.

This paper discusses the interconnection between tiny theories, such as those based on extra dimensions, and particle colliders, specifically the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). It highlights the constraints imposed by LHC data on these theories and the possibilities that emerging LHC experiments, particularly those involving smaller than standard LHC interactions or larger than standard LHC energy scales, may offer for discovering extra dimensions or other tiny components.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources, specifically those containing neutron stars, reveal patterns where the brightness fluctuates in a repetitive cycle, linked to the orbit of the star. The duration of these cycles varies significantly across different sources, often spanning months to several years. A notable exception includes sources like MXRN 1936-329 and MXRN 1916-347, whose cycle lengths are remarkably similar, approximately 93 and 86 days respectively, and show small variations. These unusual pairing of sources, along with others like MXRN 1658-487 and MXRN 1746-273, also exhibit similar cycle lengths to each other. A distinct subset within this group is characterized by short cycle lengths, often referred to as the "Z" composite, and includes sources like MXRN 1658-487, MXRN 1746-273 and MXRN 1916-329. A separate subgroup within this cycle length spectrum is the "N" composite, featuring longer cycle lengths and including sources like MXRN 1956-304, MXRN 0652-640, MXRN 0536-448 and MXRN 0538-469. A notable distinction between the "Z" and "N" composites lies in their active patterns; sources within the "Z" composite typically exhibit short, repeating patterns of brightness fluctuations interspersed with extended, invariable brightness periods, whereas sources within the "N" composite exhibit consistent, repeating patterns of brightness fluctuations

According to general relativity, the gravitational interaction between two objects affects their surrounding spacetime, which in turn impacts the motion of those objects.  This relationship constitutes the fundamental basis of the binary test of gravity.  Recent observations of binary systems that involve a compact object and a rotating neutron star have provided novel perspectives that go beyond the traditional application of the binary test.  These new viewpoints offer a comprehensive understanding of how gravity affects the neutron star's spin period and beam orientation, making binary systems that involve a compact object and a rotating neutron star $2-3$ times more effective in testing the properties of gravity than those with two compact objects. Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have varying properties depending on their optical characteristics. Research has shown a link between radio sources associated with Broad Line Radio Galaxies and those linked to Narrow Line Radio Galaxies, Radio-Galaxies without emission lines, and Seyfert Galaxies through radio source size. This study aims to broaden this understanding by examining radio source size in relation to other properties in different AGN classes, specifically those with and without core emission, broad or narrow optical emission lines, and radio sources with and without detected optical counterparts. To achieve this, we analyzed radio sources from a sample of 106 Broad Line Radio Galaxies and 306 Narrow Line Radio Galaxies. For each AGN type, we calculated the median radio source size and other characteristics. Our results indicate smaller radio source sizes in Narrow Line Radio Galaxies (median ~615.21 kpc) compared to Broad Line Radio Galaxies (median ~914.11 kpc). However, Narrow Line Radio Galaxies exhibit greater radio power (median ~10^25.55 W/Hz) than Broad Line Radio Galaxies (median ~10^24.55 W/Hz). We investigate how waves generated by massive stellar explosions, specifically fast-rising and super-Eddington explosions, interact with the surrounding envelope. As these waves move at nearly relativistic speeds through the envelope, they create a shockwave that could potentially explain various observed phenomena, such as the long-lasting radiative bumps and external shocks in supernovae, as well as dust formation in specific environments. Using numerical simulations, we examine how the generated shocks form, how energy is distributed within the envelope, and the characteristics of the waves as they break free from the gravitational well. Our analysis suggests that waves with high energies (>10^46 erg/s) could result in significant radiative cooling, while those with lower energies (<10^45 erg/s) might exhibit non-linear behavior. Furthermore, we find that waves with sufficient energy (>10^47 erg/s) could produce a second shockwave as they collide with matter ejected by the exploding star.

Additionally, we consider how these wave-shock systems could be observed from a distance and provide radiative signatures that could be used to identify such phenomena. These signatures include radiative bumps that could be associated with gamma-ray bursts without drivers, dust formation in quasipolar rings, and shockwaves that could explain long-lasting bumps following supernovae explosions.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of weight-one eigenforms to their arithmetic counterparts. 
The study is expanded to encompass weight-$k$ eigenforms, with the novel 
requirement that $k$ be greater than two. Additionally, the conditions are 
relaxed to allow for non-arithmetic weights. The approach draws upon a prior 
proof by Diamond--Sasaki, along with several key components, including a 
generalization of a theorem by Merel, a demonstration of a specific 
conjecture related to Serre's conjecture, and a specific application of 
Minardi's work on the fundamental group of the Jacobians of genus-one curves.

Molecules in motion exhibit unique interactions, primarily driven by the coupling between vibrational and electronic states, which are dependent on momentum. The advent of ultrafast spectroscopic techniques enables the study of rotating diatomic molecules in the infrared region with varying electronic states. By applying a theoretical framework that accounts for non-parabolic potential energy curves and electronic state mixing, we can 1) explain the rotational recurrence phenomenon observed in wavepackets within ground vibrational states, 2) predict spin-vibrational interference patterns in wavepackets associated with separate electronic states during rotational agitation, and 3) investigate the effects of electronic state mixing on spin-vibrational interference through momentum-space analysis.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview.

Recent advances in Natural Language Inference (NLI) have been fueled by AI models that rely on transformational representations of text. These advancements have led to proposals that pre-trained languages models (PLMs) successfully capture the semantic structure of natural language. Nonetheless, the NLI datasets commonly employed in these studies suffer from significant shortcomings, including an inadequate representation of discourse phenomena and an overly narrow focus on local text connections. This paper explores the limitations of these models in the context of semantic discourse and proposes a new evaluation framework that addresses their shortcomings. It presents a comprehensive semantic discourse dataset, incorporating 24 distinct categories of relations, along with thorough analyses of the challenges involved. This framework is found to be robust in its demands on NLI models, exceeding their current capabilities based on various metrics. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the capabilities and limitations of PLMs in interpreting the semantic context of natural language.

Automated driving technology is highly complex and susceptible to system failures due to various reasons such as poor weather conditions, mechanical malfunctions, and incorrect software updates. To ensure the safety of this technology, a robust and advanced surveillance system is crucial. Currently available surveillance systems are effective at detecting crashes and near-crashes, but they lack efficiency in predicting impending crashes. To address this shortcoming, a new algorithm called Deep Spatiotemporal Lane Change Detection network is proposed in this paper. This algorithm is designed to anticipate lane change hazards in real-time using a spatiotemporal fusion approach and features such as lane detection, optical flow, and mask transfer. Furthermore, the proposed method is capable of detecting hazards even in the presence of distracting scenes following a training protocol designed to simulate natural data distribution. Experimental results indicate that this algorithm is not only precise but also efficient in predicting lane change hazards and detecting actual crashes during validation and testing phases.

The notion that massive objects must be spinning slowly to remain in equilibrium under gravity, as expressed through angular momentum conservation, is widely accepted. This concept is particularly relevant to massive objects like black holes and neutron stars that are formed from the collapse of massive stars. The process of compact binary merger also creates neutron stars and black holes with significant angular momentum. Research has demonstrated that these objects can enter binary systems via this pathway, rather than through the collapse of single stars. The rules that govern the rotation of such objects in their early stages of formation are not yet fully understood. The simulation of rotating stars with masses below Chandrasekhar limits, throughout their entire evolutionary stages, is the objective of this research. The stars simulated ranged from 0.1 to 0.90 in mass, with various chemical compositions, in both single-star and binary-star scenarios. The simulation allowed for Roche-lobe overflow and common envelope neutron star and black hole production. The resulting objects were spun up to their barycentric velocities in lopsided binaries, as well as in neutron star and black hole binary mergers. The upper limits of stable Maupertuisian rotation in stellar models are novel findings of this research. The amplitude assessment technique, widely used to evaluate seismic ground motion data, is highly dependent on experimental measurements. However, the current method of presentation fails to effectively convey the uncertainty associated with these measurements, which are critical for a thorough understanding of results. The proposed uncertainty factor $f_{\sigma}$ is designed to express the variability of different measurement sets and is defined as the standard deviation of individual components divided by the square root of the number of components. This quantity is a more intuitive indicator of uncertainty than traditional metrics and is influenced by the characteristics of both the input data and the assessment method. As a result, $f_{\sigma}$ is capable of reflecting the uncertainty associated with amplitude assessments across distinct frequency ranges. Therefore, it is essential to consider $f_{\sigma}$ when interpreting results, as it is an essential component of the amplitude assessment method. Furthermore, $f_{\sigma}$ is sensitive to the choice of frequency range, which is a crucial consideration for amplitude assessment.

A new comprehensive framework is introduced, enabling a detailed exploration of long GRB afterglows in an uniform radiative framework that distinguishes between radiative and non-radiative components. This framework, which incorporates radiative radiations, synchrocompton radiations, and synchroselfcompton radiations, bridges the gap between radiative and non-radiative radiations through synchrocompton radiations. This framework offers a dynamic perspective on GRB afterglows, allowing for a thorough examination of radiations across various radiative components, and for the first time makes possible a dynamic study of GRB afterglows in the context of radiative, synchrocompton, synchroselfcompton radiations within a global radiative components framework.

In graph theory, a popular problem is the Bipartite Vertex Partition problem, which seeks to determine whether a given graph can be divided into two components using a specific rule. Researchers have previously demonstrated an exact solution using a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the graph's treewidth. Building upon this work, we present a new algorithm utilizing the graph's treewidth as a parameter, which yields a solution for a broader class of bipartite vertex partition problems. Specifically, we can divide graphs using multiple rules as long as these rules do not conflict with each other. This algorithm runs within the confines of the parameter and the graph's size, with the time complexity defined by $O(2^{k} \, poly(\ell) \, verbatim{dpoly}(n))$. Here, $k$ represents the number of rules being applied, $\ell$ represents the maximum degree of any vertex, and $n$ represents the graph's number of vertices.

Deep neural network classifiers have excelled in various tasks but may struggle with the challenge of incremental learning across multiple categories. A significant obstacle in this domain is the issue of categorial imbalancing, where some classes are learned before others. This problem is encountered in several real-world applications such as image recognition and anomaly detection, where data is constantly being updated with new features that are not necessarily balanced. The goal of research in this area is centered around achieving high performance overall by developing algorithms that effectively manage memory and maintain a balance between older and newer learned classes. This paper focuses on the specific issue of incremental learning across multiple categories where some classes are learned before others and presents a comprehensive evaluation of various calibration techniques to address the issue of categorial imbalancing. After conducting extensive experiments on several datasets, the results show that incorporating a simple technique called 'exponential calibration' leads to significant improvements in performance. The code for the paper has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This paper will present a method to enhance the resilience and efficiency of bipedal robots during their gait cycle by providing additional power through ankle actuation. A kinetic energy-based assessment of the energy dynamics will be used to create a reduced-order bipedal walking model, which will enable the derivation of stability and performance metrics within the closed loop. To generate proprietary data for the model, a novel approach that leverages publicly available information will be presented. The efficacy of the proposed approach will be validated through simulations and experiments with a reduced-scale humanoid robot. The findings of this research will contribute to the development of efficient and resilient bipedal robots capable of navigating uneven terrain.

We provide a detailed explanation of a highly specialized concept from algebraic geometry, specifically within the context of residue symbols and weak approximation for algebraic tori over number fields. Our analysis focuses on the conditions required for a family of places to enable the construction of local fields that are linked to a given set of global fields via isomorphisms preserving residues. In this context, we identify the necessary and sufficient criteria for such place families to exist for any given set of global fields, thereby establishing a connection between the fields themselves. This connection enables the construction of local fields that are closely related to the original algebraic tori over number fields, allowing for the application of descent techniques to prove the validity of the Descent Density Conjecture for algebraic tori over number fields. Consequently, our results imply that the Conjecture holds true for any algebraic tori defined over the rational numbers or over number fields with a fundamental group that is abelian in nature.

Recent studies have uncovered substantial differences in how various instruction sets, such as AVX-512, NEON, and ARMv8, manage memory operations that access aligned bytes within a 128-bit word. While porting a workload to a more efficient instruction set can lead to significant performance gains, doing so often results in a considerable increase in memory traffic, counteracting the benefits. To address this issue, this work proposes HyperDegrade, an instruction set architecture transformation approach that aims to enhance performance without compromising energy efficiency. By incorporating a layer that bridges the gap between memory accesses and instruction sets, HyperDegrade enables the utilization of wider registers and instruction sets while minimizing memory traffic. To demonstrate its effectiveness, this work showcases the implementation of HyperDegrade for a specific workload, achieving a 5.5$\times$ performance improvement and a 3.6$\times$ energy efficiency boost on a state-of-the-art CPU, compared to an energy-efficient NEON-based implementation. Furthermore, HyperDegrade's potential is illustrated by showing that similar performance gains can be achieved for various memory-intensive applications, resulting in a 2.5$\times$ to 5.5$\times$ improvement in performance, a 2$\times$ to 3.6$\times$ improvement in energy efficiency, and a 10% to 30% reduction in memory traffic.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a statistical tool to assess the risks involved. This analysis was carried out within the framework of a highly constrained Standard Model with a Higgs (cSMH) using the existing ATLAS and ALICE datasets. The Higgs contribution to the anomaly is significant, with a probability of occurrence of 95.5%. However, the uncertainty associated with this finding is substantial, and it cannot be ruled out that the Higgs might account for the anomaly with a probability of as low as 10%. The conditions for the Higgs to account for the anomaly at a 95% confidence level are as follows: the Higgs must contribute at least 50% of the anomaly, and its contribution must be within the range of 1.3 sigma standard deviations. If the Higgs is responsible for the anomaly, it would imply that the Higgs mass is greater than the expected value by a range of 1.5 to 3.5 sigma standard deviations. The Higgs contribution to the anomaly could be confirmed or ruled out with approximately 290 ab^-1 of integrated luminosity, assuming the LHC reaches an integrated luminosity of 3 ab^-1 per year.

The disintegration of heavy particles into photons and matter particles at a point where these particles interact quickly, can be used to determine how these particles interact with each other. By analyzing the decay of heavy particles that are not observable, like top quarks, this information can be inferred to study the disintegration of heavier particles, such as Higgs bosons, more accurately. In the context of the Standard Model, the self-interaction of the Higgs boson can be understood through the disintegration of heavy particles that are not observable, like top quarks, and it primarily affects the rate of the Higgs boson decaying into two photons or photons and other matter particles. In the case of the Standard Model, this process is very well measured, but it is not the case for models that go beyond the Standard Model where the self-interaction of the Higgs boson with a heavy top quark is more complex and needs a more precise definition of how these particles interact with each other to determine parameters like the coupling between the Higgs boson and two photons or photons and other matter particles correctly. In the case of the Standard Model, the self-interaction of the Higgs boson with a heavy top quark is so strong that it affects the rate of the Higgs boson decaying into two photons or photons and other matter particles in a way that is dependent on the energy of the photons and it is not the case for models that go beyond the Standard Model where this relationship

A new method has been developed for releasing knots from any given link configuration, in both traditional and welded settings. A specific set of rules, applied in a sequential manner, guarantees successful unknotting of any knot. This process involves minimizing crossings and attaching a simple loop to specific X-chunk regions of the link. A key aspect of the algorithm is its universality, as it effectively unknots even the most complex knots, including those with arbitrarily large bridge indices and intertwined double knots.
We demonstrate that the set of tropical functions from a curve to the real numbers is topologically finite when the parameter of non-differentiability is changed.

Given any oriented link L in the ambient space R^3, we can establish a specific set of polynomials, denoted as the Jones polynomials, through the use of a particular sequence of transformations called the n-fold integral with respect to a specific variable, u. By applying a particular transformation to the 2-fold integral of the Jones polynomial of an oriented link L with respect to the variable u, we can derive a value, denoted as J2(L), which is invariant to changes in the link's configuration. By defining a particular differential form, denoted as δ, and evaluating it for an oriented link L using a specific set of coordinates, we can derive a value, denoted as ∫L, which is linked to J2(L) through the use of Fox-Hatcher's 1-cocycle, β. By establishing a particular relationship between the differential form, δ, and Fox-Hatcher's 1-cocycle, β, we can demonstrate that the value, ∫L, is a Vassiliev invariant of order three for an oriented link L.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides a significantly low neutrino mass limit of approximately 0.8 eV. To understand the implications of this finding, we examined multiple scenarios using three distinct models: the first includes only neutrino mass, the second incorporates neutrino and Higgs boson interactions, and the third adds Higgs boson interactions in addition to constraints from electroweak precision. Through an analysis of an extensive set of operators within the Standard Model, we identified the most restrictive paradigms that satisfy the conditions set by the KATRIN collaboration. Our research demonstrates that even with the most recent low-bias statistics from KATRIN, we can set an upper limit of approximately 0.23 GeV on the total neutrino mass. This finding holds significant importance in theoretical models that predict the maximum possible neutrino mass-to-dark matter ratio, which could be as low as 0.25 in a few scenarios. Moreover, we discovered that even with the most recent lumen factor constraint, we can set an upper limit of approximately 14 GeV on the axion mass. This research also provides the most recent low-bias statistics for the electron neutrino background, which could be as low as 0.22 MeV, a value that could be confirmed by upcoming electron voltage spectrometers.

Nesta apresentação, exploraremos as técnicas de multiplicação de matrizes, que são fundamentais em diversas aplicativas, incluindo redes neuronais. As abordagens paralelas e sequenciais para este cálculo serão comparadas, com foco nas características das arquiteturas de processamento sequencial (CPU) e paralelo (GPU) e como elas afetam o desempenho no cálculo de matrizes. Além disso, discutiremos como a organização da memória afeta a eficiência nas operações de multiplicação de matrizes.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, the key to success often lies in the interplay between their collaborative actions and the structure of their surrounding environment. To make decisions in such situations, optimal policies typically require significant computation, information exchange, and planning capabilities. However, many practical applications, like multi-robot search and rescue scenarios, often involve a large number of simple agents working together to achieve complex goals within an unknown environment. The existing literature on multi-agent decision-making theories offers little in terms of scalable, distributed solutions suitable for these kinds of situations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach based on collaborative learning among robots with limited computation and communication capabilities in a time-varying network. Our algorithm enables each robot to make decisions using a high-level policy that can handle uncertainty and environment complexity, despite only having access to local sensory information and limited information from neighboring robots. The resulting policy is a collaborative product of the robots' individual efforts, allowing them to achieve up to a 10 times improvement in performance compared to non-cooperative behavior, as demonstrated in a multi-robot navigation task. The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/awaiskhattak/SMAC.

In quantum field theory, perturbation theory is compromised by scale issues, primarily due to the high sensitivity of field scales in the theory's parameters. This limitation is addressed by switching to amplitude-based perturbation, which is less sensitive to scale changes. This new approach is made accessible through a set of infrared-accurate functions, achieving a level of precision that is achievable when the degree of divergence in amplitudes is taken into consideration. Our research reveals that the degree of divergence is a bridge that connects infrared and ultraviolet aspects of amplitudes and, in an IR-driven analysis, amplitude components are distinguished based on their infrared properties. This distinction enables the separation of IR and UV scales within amplitudes, allowing for the definition of IR- and UV-driven functions. Our research also shows that the degree of divergence is a determining factor in the behavior of IR-driven functions in various scaling limits, which find a clear reflection in the properties of Cornwall function. In a series of lectures, we will delve into IR-driven analysis, focusing on the properties of amplitude components, the degree of divergence, and its role in the scaling behavior of IR-driven functions within amplitude-based perturbation. This will include a discussion on the challenges related to the implementation of amplitude-based perturbation in quantum field theory, particularly within the context of renormalization theory.

As the concept of federated learning gains momentum, various industries are exploring ways to tackle challenging problems through a collaborative approach. In the educational sector, an emerging trend called vertical federated learning enables multiple institutions to collaborate on data-intensive analytics projects. However, the success of VFL relies heavily on the cooperation of institutions, which are often driven by a desire for improved security and data protection. In this paper, we expose a type of attack that takes advantage of the inherent nature of VFL and aim to undermine the privacy of students by manipulating the collaborative process. We also present a novel attack framework and demonstrate its effectiveness through a simulation study, finding that neural network-based VFL can be vulnerable to significant errors. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under the Neven-You influence attack and prove mathematically that the attack's impact is directly related to the dataset's size. Additionally, we explore various countermeasure techniques, such as data preprocessing, ensemble methods, and regularization, to enhance the robustness of VFL against such attacks.

Kernel based methods, renowned for their versatility in approximating diverse algorithms like Support Vector Machines and Dynamic Programming, often employ matrix techniques to expedite computation. However, kernel based methods run into scalability issues when dealing with large datasets. Approximation techniques, such as Random Fourier Features, provide a feasible solution by treating kernels as linear functions. Despite being computationally efficient, the accuracy of such approximations depends on the choice of feature number. This research introduces an alternative kernel estimation framework, based on the attributes of signals in the Random Fourier Domain, which produces more accurate approximations with a significantly reduced number of features. The method's performance is under the control of a theoretical per feature bias, per feature variance and an empirical bias variance. The method is further augmented with a technique to reduce variance by utilizing multiple iterations. The method is evaluated on high dimensional data and outperforms the state of the art in literature.

The study introduces a new approach to embedding groups into matrix groups within the framework of Cartesian Decomposition. This method differs from previous techniques used for solvable groups and provides a universal strategy for groups with a solvable subgroup. The approach is particularly useful for groups with a nilpotent subgroup as it allows the decomposition of the identity element into a specific form, which can be further utilized to derive a series expansion for group elements. The study demonstrates that both the unitary group U(n) and the general linear group GL(n) can be embedded into a series of matrix groups through the CD method. The paper also presents the Lie algebra representation of the CD system and demonstrates that the CD system corresponds to a specific type of quadratic algebra, which ultimately leads to the decomposition of the identity element into a specific form. The form can be further utilized to derive a series expansion for group elements, which is displayed in the paper.

This research paper examines whether a specific condition, namely that a compact hypersurface in n-dimensional space has a certain property called M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility, is necessary for it to be geodesically complete. To approach this question, the authors first investigate what it means for a compact hypersurface in n-dimensional space to have M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility and then determine that it is equivalent to it having constant M\"obius curvature. They then look at the specific case of a compact, smooth hypersurface in (n+1)-dimensional space and show that it has M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility if and only if it has constant M\"obius curvature. Next, the authors explore whether this condition is sufficient for the surface to be geodesically complete and find that it is not, as they are able to construct examples of compact, smooth hypersurfaces in (n+1)-dimensional space with constant M\"obius curvature that are not geodesically complete. However, the authors are also able to show that if the compact, smooth hypersurface in (n+1)-dimensional space has constant M\"obius curvature and is also locally convex, then it is geodesically complete.

In congenital heart disease, pre-surgery planning is a critical step in treatment, and medical professionals use detailed cardiac MRI scans for this process. Automatic segmentation of cardiac structures from these MRI scans has the potential to significantly streamline this process. However, there's a notable lack of data associated with congenital heart defects, which poses a challenge for evaluating the practicality of this method on a clinical scale. We've discovered that a relatively basic implementation of a U-Net architecture is capable of accurately identifying main cardiac structures from MRI scans with high precision and speed, even in cases of complex congenital heart defects such as hypoplastic left heart syndrome and tetralogy of Fallot. Moreover, we found that models trained on adult data aren't a suitable alternative, due to significant reductions in performance. Furthermore, we've shown that a level of semantic segmentation is possible, which is a more advanced technique than the traditional approach used, and that this method is sufficiently fast for practical use.

This study explores a range of materials, from brittle solids to soft and sticky fluids, with the common characteristic of exhibiting stress gradients. The stress gradients in these materials are associated with the spatial variation of shear stress within parallel surfaces that are sliding past each other. The model proposed here links the microscale behavior at the interface to macroscopic stress gradients. It postulates that stress gradients cause a movement along the interface, which in turn generates a force opposing the slip between adjacent points. The model's simplicity allows it to be represented mathematically as a specific type of differential equation. The proposed model applies to any material where the energy spent to create a unit length of crack is independent of the crack's length. The model also offers a way to determine the velocity at which a pre-existing crack propagates. It demonstrates that the stress near a curved crack in an infinite space of air follows the same patterns as the stress near a sharp corner, albeit with the difference that the stress near a curved crack is affected by the radius of the curve. The model further shows that the stress near a flat crack in an infinite space of air is similar to the stress near a notch, albeit with the difference that the stress near a flat crack is affected by the width of the crack. The model also provides a way to determine the radius of a circular crack given its location within a material of known curvature or to determine the curvature of a crack given its location within a material of known radius.
