A significant portion of the universe's massive star population remains unobserved through optical telescopes due to their location within nuclear star clusters. However, recent discoveries have revealed that these clusters host numerous intermediate-mass black holes, thereby providing a possible means of detecting gravitational waves. Using a combination of astrophysical and gravitational wave data, researchers can determine the population's characteristics and understand the universe's population of massive stars. Nuclear star clusters are comprised of $10^{10}$ times more massive stars than galaxy Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) samples, and their population features include intermediate-mass black holes and neutron star binaries that emit gravitational waves. These clusters produce twice as many binary black hole mergers as the extragalactic population, with merger rates that span a range of $0.01$ to $1.00 per century within a specific binary configuration. These findings provide a more substantial foundation for future gravitational wave detectors like the upgraded LIGO and the future Square Kilometre Array radio telescope, which will greatly increase their capability to study the population of nuclear star clusters.

The rapid response to Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and their origins significantly depends on the capabilities of early and accurate spacecraft-borne localization systems. To optimize effectiveness, it is crucial to thoroughly assess the performance of these systems, particularly their ability to determine GRB directions. A modular, semi-realistic GRB simulator has been developed to evaluate and test the Gamma-Ray Burst Detection and Localization Demonstration (GEDAD) system of the China's Hard X-ray Transient Patrol (CHAITN) mission. The simulator, simulated using a Gamma-Ray Burst ground reference, is based on the spectrum and characteristics of GRBs observed by the CHAITN/ Gedad. The simulator's performance was evaluated during its testing phase. The results show that the simulator is capable of simulating a wide range of GRBs that match Gedad's performance characteristics, including its detector configuration, energy and spectral resolution, and ability to detect and localize GRBs in real-time. The evaluation of the Gedad system using the simulator showed accurate results, with an average angular error of around 5.76 degrees, and a maximum error of 11.56 degrees, that matches international standards for GRB localization systems. The GRB simulator provides real-time, high-fidelity data that mimics the performance of GRB detectors on board spacecraft, making it an invaluable tool for the testing, evaluation, and calibration of GRB localization systems.

This article investigates a range of composition operators and their associated integral operators within specific complex function spaces, including BMOA and its associated subspace, and confirms that a semigroup of such operators is bounded when acting on the respective space. Building on existing research by Anderson and MacGregor, specific cases are considered for the Zhukov operator and the d/a operator when acting on BMOA and its subspace. Additionally, definitions are provided for a broader class of composition operators and their associated integral operators, along with corresponding bounds for a semigroup of such operators within the given complex function spaces.

Researchers within the information retrieval and machine learning fields often rely on benchmark datasets that are typically compiled from scientific literature. Conversely, studies set within the information-based framework rarely examine scientific literature as a whole. In contrast to such practices, our research delves into analysis of all scholarly articles published worldwide, utilizing CiteSeerX as our primary source. With over 800,000 papers indexed, our analysis reveals insights into categories of science that are actively producing, have previously produced significant output, and are notably underrepresented. We develop a quantitative metric to gauge the disparateness between categories in terms of output and previous knowledge contributions. Ultimately, we utilize this metric to identify underrepresented fields and demonstrate the effectiveness of inducing neutral word embeddings in relation to the neutral metric. Through our approach, we are able to differentiate the performance of neutral word embeddings over time and validate the accuracy of our findings through additional analyses and explicit feedback from experts within the identified fields.

In this research, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use co-operative relaying technology over systems employing Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) technology is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the security performance of Systems Employing Multiple Carriers (SEMC) with co-operative relaying. To evaluate the effectiveness of co-operative relaying in protecting system physical layers, we develop an analytical model for the probability distribution function (pdf) of the cumulative interference power in SEMC systems employing the co-operative relay protocol. To validate the analytical findings, we conduct a series of Monte Carlo simulations. To further enhance the physical layer security of SEMC systems using co-operative relaying, we propose modifying the system to use a co-operative relay protocol with a Nash equilibrium power allocation strategy. To evaluate the effectiveness of this proposed strategy, we develop an analytical model for the pdf of the cumulative interference power in SEMC systems employing the proposed protocol. To facilitate easier design of SEMC systems employing the proposed protocol, we also develop a closed-form expression for the system's security performance metric. To further validate the findings related to the proposed protocol, we conduct a series of Monte Carlo simulations.

Quantum electrodynamics enables the non-linear interaction between photons and matter. In waveguide quantum electrodynamics, this interaction is utilized through semi-conductor micro-resonators that form part of a waveguide, allowing for the enabling of multi-channel, non-local quantum operations between different points. Building on previous work, we now consider the topological aspect of this phenomenon by incorporating photonic topological insulators into the setup. This modification creates non-Abelian effective interactions between photons across separate channels, thereby producing complex, entangled states from single photon excitations. Furthermore, this system facilitates the realization of non-Abelian gauge transformations through optical operations alone, a feature that cannot be achieved with conventional strategies.

The integration of automated vehicles into existing mixed traffic networks holds great promise for improving efficiency and reducing road-related accidents. To tackle the complex safety challenges associated with this transition, a data-driven approach to predictive management for automated vehicles is proposed, focusing on critical signalized intersection points. This method leverages real-time data and historical information to model intersection dynamics and pedestrian behavior, enabling the development of safety-critical trajectories for linked automated vehicles. Through simulation testing, the proposed system's effectiveness is demonstrated in reducing rear-end collisions between human-driven and automated vehicles at an intersection, and pedestrian impact is also mitigated.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One notable issue with existing text-based games, however, is their slow speed, which significantly hampers the testing process and the evaluation of agents.
To address this limitation, we present TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three popular text-based games, including TextWorld, MultiAgentTextWorld, FillingKitchen, and Cursed, with the goal of enabling rapid testing and evaluation of agent performance.
By leveraging a range of advanced techniques including asynchronous updates, linear layer architectures, and pre-trained embeddings, TextWorldExpress achieves speeds of up to one million moves per second on a single GPU, which is nearly two orders of magnitude faster than the original games.

In recent years, Deep Learning, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have gained popularity in image and video recognition tasks. However, the significant computational requirements and energy consumption associated with these models on hardware like Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) create significant barriers to their implementation. To address this issue, we propose an energy-efficient LSTM network based on a Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTD) structure, which reduces model size and computational complexity while maintaining high accuracy levels. A comprehensive algorithm was developed to optimize the network's latency, area, and energy consumption. When put to the test on the VMVR-INDENT video recognition dataset, our proposed HTTD-LSTM model demonstrated superior accuracy (96.56%) compared to other decomposition-based models, as well as reduced energy consumption (65.6%) and a significant improvement (25.9%) in energy-efficiency per inference.

Recent studies incorporating partial information on supervised learning models have shown significant potential in accurately processing real-world data. Despite the progress made, research into the subject remains limited, primarily due to the absence of comprehensive datasets that incorporate partial information in a controlled manner. To bridge this gap, the project presents datasets comprising overlapping text that serve as inputs for two distinct tasks - summarization and question-answering. Additionally, the study examines the finding that supervised learning models perform better when provided with more comprehensive information that includes irrelevant content. To to overcome this limitation, the project proposes an alternative approach that involves conditioning the models on relevant information alone, leading to improved performance when evaluated against the information restriction test. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the benefits of conditioning are both model-agnostic, applying to various types of models, and robust to changes in model parameters. The results suggest that NLP models can sometimes perform suboptimally when exposed to excessive information and that the achievement of optimal performance relies on the interplay between model capacity and the quality of the input information.

We investigate a subset of stationary states in a conformally invariant system under the influence of a source that represents gravity. Specifically, we explore states that carry a specific charge and are located within a specific spatial region. Initially, we demonstrate that, for a specific type of source, states with the highest degree of symmetry will minimize the energy under conformally invariant transformations. This finding leads to the conclusion that states with higher degrees of symmetry will, in descending order, minimize the energy for other types of sources that represent gravity, which is akin to a form of the weak null hypothesis in the context of the Feeble Gravity Conjecture. Building upon this result, we go on to show that the same logic applied to the source that represents gravity will imply that the energy will be minimized by states with the highest degree of symmetry under conformally invariant transformations, which is a stronger condition. This line of reasoning suggests that the property of having a highest symmetry state for a specific source implies the same condition for all sources, which could potentially be a feature that is universal across systems that are invariant under the Poincaré group.

To efficiently tackle the significant computational challenges associated with large-scale quantum simulations, it is crucial to limit the number of regions where the system is divided for observation and control. Our study proposes an ideal framework for dividing the system into multiple regions by utilizing a model-space quantum imaginary duration evolution (MQIDE) approach, which combines the advantages of the quantum imaginary time evolution method and the algebraic quantum imaginary time propagation technique. This model-space approach involves defining a set of correlated model-space orbits that capture the overall structure of the Hamiltonian, and then conducting independent quantum simulations within each of these regions. By incorporating local particle and hole condensate operators into the Hamiltonian, as well as introducing region-specific chemical potentials, we are able to induce condensate formation in each model space through imaginary time evolution. We demonstrate that the wavefunction obtained using this approach is consistent with that from the exact diagonalization method for a specific example involving a single particle within a three-dimensional cube with harmonic potential, and further show that the MQIDE approach is robust against changes in the model-space orbitals by illustrating the imaginary time evolution of a particle confined to an s-orbital within a hydrogen atom. Finally, we apply the MQIDE approach to study the imaginary time evolution of a single electron within a hydrogenic atom, and find that it yields results inconsistent with the requirements of the K\"all\'en-Lehmann spectral representation, highlighting the need for further improvement of this model-space approach.

In this study, we establish a connection between two critical properties of local rings: Finiteness of Dimension, as characterized by a compact Hilbert polynomial, and F-rationality. We investigate how links of F-rational local rings relate to Gorenstein local rings, specifically examining how the former's F-rationality is influenced by their local dimension. Additionally, we explore a related conjecture related to Artin van der Werden's conjecture regarding the dimension of local rings.

The Auxiliary Services Procurement Model exploits big data to understand market dynamics, leveraging a range of techniques including agent-based modeling, computational economics, and data science. 

The problem it addresses is related to the development of innovative procurement approaches for auxiliary services, such as cloud computing and cybersecurity, which are critical to the success of large projects like the European Union's Horizon 2020. 

The model uses a novel procuring organization agent-based model, which simulates the interactions between public buyers and private service providers to analyze the outcomes of different procurement strategies.

The approach to development is characterized by a multi-disciplinary approach, involving collaboration between academics and public sector experts, and an iterative development process, with a focus on realism and feasibility.

The case study presented involves the development of a demonstration system for the procurement of cloud services, which involves a complex web of relationships between 1,000 providers and 10 major buyer organizations.

The outcome of the project is a working demonstration system, which is available for download and can be used as a starting point for further development and refinement.

The paper concludes with an outline of potential areas for extension and refinement, including the integration of financial aspects and the development of more complex provider organizations.

R.W.K. Odoni initially observed that some entire functions of a specific form have a prime focus. We expand upon this by showing that certain functions of a combined polynomial nature also exhibit a prime focus. In addition, we find that the dynamics of a specific type of combined polynomial are linked to the dynamics of a related family of polynomials through iterative applications.

To study the production of Higgs boson pairs at the Large Hadron Collider, a new method called the matrix element technique is being explored to improve identification of these events. By utilizing this method, events resulting in the creation of a Higgs boson pair decaying into two bottom quarks and a boson and a virtual W boson, are more effectively distinguished from other events based on experimental data from the CMS detector. A study was conducted to determine the efficiency of this method, specifically how it identifies events resulting in the creation of a Higgs boson pair decaying into two bottom quarks and two W bosons, and finds that this method is more efficient than current techniques. The study also determines the sensitivity of this method to various factors such as the energy at which the particles are detected and the characteristics of the proton beam used in the experiments.

We investigate how accurately the reaction $e^+e^- \to Zh$ can determine the parameters of an extended scalar sector with multiple Higgs fields, specifically focusing on a minimal $SU(2)_L$ invariant model with three Higgs fields. We discovered that in this model, the reaction $e^+e^- \to Zh$ is highly sensitive to the degeneracy $\epsilon$ among the Higgs boson masses at future $e^+e-$ colliders, with an accuracy that can determine $\epsilon$ with an error of less than $10^{-3}$ ($10^{-2}$) at the CEPC (FCC-ee). Furthermore, we found that the combination of $e^+e^- \to Zh$ and $h \to \gamma \gamma$ at the CEPC (FCC-ee) can simultaneously determine the Higgs self-coupling and the light Higgs-stray coupling with an accuracy of $10^{-3}$ ($10^{-2}$), assuming that the Higgs decay to two photons is already serving as a standard candle for checking the scalability and accuracy of Higgs physics at future $e^+e-$ colliders.

Observations of a rare atmospheric phenomenon, a six-sided weather pattern called a hexagon, have been ongoing for over two decades around Saturn. Conducted using the Cassini spacecraft, these observations took place around the planet's summer solstice in the north. During this time, a significant atmospheric occurrence in Saturn's polar regions is formation of polar vortices, which are isolated areas of rotating and spinning air. However, the process is challenging to study due to the slow timescales involved. Using data from the radio science system and the infrared spectrometer, researchers analyzed changes in Saturn's atmospheric atmosphere around the North Polar Hexagon. They investigated whether the formation of the polar vortex in Saturn's northern hemisphere during its summer was influenced by the presence of the hexagon. However, their research indicates that the vortex formed too slowly to be influenced by the hexagon's characteristics. It instead formed in a more stable atmospheric section of Saturn. Nevertheless, the team discovered a more substantial atmospheric wave that could have originated from the hexagon and contributed to the vortex's formation. This finding sheds light on the intricate relationship between Saturn's wave-driven circulation and the characteristics of the North Polar Hexagon. It also reveals the importance of considering this relationship in the study of planetary wave patterns around Saturn.

This study focuses on the Schrödinger equation under specific conditions and identifies certain solution behaviors in areas outside of a convex shape. A particular type of solution, explosive in nature, is found to occur under certain circumstances within these areas. It has been determined that within these areas, solutions can take on an explosive form of decay, and this explosive decay rate is directly linked to the imaginary part of the spectrum in a specific range. It was also discovered that within these areas, solutions can take on an explosive form of growth, and this explosive growth rate is also directly linked to the imaginary part of the spectrum in a different range. A key finding of this study is that within these areas, solutions can take on both an explosive form of growth and decay, and these solutions can be linked to the spectral mapping theorem. It was also demonstrated that under certain harmonic extensions, solutions can take on an explosive form of growth and decay in areas outside of a convex shape, and that this can occur even when the absolute value of the spectrum is less than one. A major breakthrough of this study is the identification of solutions under certain conditions within these areas, and it paves the way for further exploration of solution behaviors in areas outside of a convex shape.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-based, semi-parametric abbreviations for a wide range of polynomial equations over a specific class of $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras hold true in a context of positive characteristic. Additionally, our findings extend to a broader class of finite $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras, encompassing those generated by a finite set of elements, within a specific characteristic.

The unusual properties of V$_2$O$_3$ are attributed to its unique metal-insulator phase transitions, which can be influenced by surface modifications in epitaxially grown thin films.  Investigating these effects, we employed in situ soft x-ray photoemission spectroscopy and surface x-ray scattering during cooling down from the aerosilylytically grown V$_2$O$_3$ (0001) ultrathin films, and discovered that oxygen vacancies on the surface trigger a metal-insulator transition at a higher temperature than inside the material.  Additionally, vacuum annealing allowed us to control the quantity of these vacancies to study their impact, and we discovered that a specific vacancy arrangement can shift the metal-insulator transition to the same temperature as the bulk, and we also found that the phase transition is mediated by the volume change associated with the oxidation of V$^{3+}$ to V$^{4+}$.  These findings provide a foundation for a better comprehension of the intricate correlations between the electronic and structural properties of V$_2$O$_3$, and the influence of surface modifications on the metal-insulator transition in this material.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise finite-size dependence of these fractions in ground states by accurately calculating the partition function for quantum double dark-soliton states in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we investigate the dynamics of these states by developing an exact expression for the momentum distribution in quantum double dark-soliton states at finite time increments. This shows how these states evolve into quasi-condensed states that resemble ground states in a scaled form.

We've discovered a new property in sets with a specific ordering, which guarantees a notable connection to the concept of submodularity. This innovation enables us to make significant contributions to two critical areas: maximizing the sum of non-negative functions, and approximating NP-hard objectives using a 'halving' algorithm. Our results include an efficient algorithm for minimizing the maximum occurring frequency in a graded collection, as well as a 2-factor approximation algorithm for maximizing a submodular function subject to polynomially-sized constraints. Additionally, we've derived a 2-factor approximation algorithm for solving NP-hard problems that have a natural formulation in terms of graded collections, via a simple reduction.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the standardization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they connect to the Tamagawa measure. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the relationship between the Tamagawa measure and the product of local measures in the context of GL2.

To fully grasp the intricate dynamics of quantum systems, it is essential to monitor both their amplitude and phase properties in a unified measurement process. While amplitude information can be derived from resonant x-ray scattering, recovering phase information is far more complicated. A technique called nuclear phase recovery spectroscopy has been developed to address this challenge. This method involves utilizing the circular dichroism signal in x-ray emission from aligned nuclear moments to determine the phase. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical modeling and simulated data analysis based on a specific example involving the M\"{o}ssbauer nucleus $^{57}$Fe. The example shows that precise recovery of the phase is possible, even with low-intensity signals and significant noise. The development of this technique is especially relevant for studying quantum systems using intense x-ray pulses at high brightness x-ray facilities.

In the realm of quantum computing, error correction is a critical function that ensures the stability of operational quantum processors. Referencing the work of Shor, this function can be achieved through topological quantum error correction, which is performed via quantum error correction codes that tolerate impurities and noise during quantum computations. Currently, research focuses on implementing these codes using quantum error correction circuits that incorporate classical spin models, thereby leveraging the established understanding of these models to assess the efficacy of such implementations. Nonetheless, a crucial aspect that remains unexplored in this research is the existence of a "threshold" – a specific error rate below which quantum error correction is demonstrably capable of preventing computation errors, as demonstrated through numerical simulations employing the classical 2D toric code model. Interestingly, this threshold is found to be significantly influenced by the method of quantum error correction, with varying values ranging from 5.57% to 13.52%, and intriguingly, a notable disparity is observed between the theoretical upper limit of this threshold (which is 5.56%) and the highest obtained value among the tested quantum error correction circuits (which is 12.19%), indicating that the currently employed circuit architectures fail to achieve the optimal theoretical performance, thereby providing a basis for further optimizations of quantum error correction circuits.

Researchers propose a new method to control the properties of tellurene, a topological insulator, by functionalizing its surface with different atoms and molecules. Utilizing theoretical calculations and experimental measurements with Scanning Tunneling Microscopy, they demonstrate the capacity to tailor the electronic and structural characteristics of tellurene. Specifically, they show that functionalizing tellurene with fluorine and sulfur results in significant changes to its surface structure and electronic properties. These changes lead to enlarged gaps in the energy spectrum, making the material even more suitable for applications requiring large gaps. The team also finds that sulfur-functionalized tellurene maintains its original three-dimensional stability, whereas the same functionalization causes a shift to two-dimensional stability in molybdenum disulfide. These findings open up the possibility of using sulfur-functionalized tellurene as a stable and versatile material for topological surface states.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced that combines distinct finite element methods to model single-phase Darcy flow within highly permeable rock with fractures. Based on the hydraulic fracture's thickness, two finite element techniques are utilized: a conforming method for thin fractures and an isogeometric collocation method for thicker fractures. A hybrid technique was then developed to solve the mixed problem, involving discontinuous pressure and Dirac delta functions, to determine the flow rate and storage properties within each fracture type. Several tests, including scenarios with fractures of varying thickness and curvature, and comparisons with established analytical solutions, have been conducted to validate the proposed method.

A spiral magnetic layer without an external magnetic field possesses unique properties that can enable a solitary "domain" of superconductivity, and this domain is controllable through an external transverse magnetic field. Research indicates that changing the spiral magnetic structure can precisely achieve this control. Interestingly, studies have discovered that replacing the spiral magnetic layer with a specific type of antiferromagnetic layer doesn't enable superconductivity in the same way. However, surprising insights emerge when considering specific alignments of the layer's magnetic structure, revealing that superconductivity might also be controlled in this alternative setup. This finding raises the possibility that using different types of spiral layers could lead to even more sophisticated functions in a superconducting spin switch.

In statistical model selection, Bayes factors are widely regarded as an effective metric to compare competing models. However, the complexity of modern computational simulations often hinders the routine use of Bayes factors, due to the necessity for multiple model specifications and the consequent need for simultaneous analysis across models. This study investigates the advantages of using a flexible, specification-free approach to estimate Bayes factors via workflow strategies, leveraging the versatility of the MCMCest package. Our results demonstrate that this approach surpasses traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, reducing the bias in Bayes factor estimates by approximately 75% and outperforming them by two orders of magnitude in computational time. This study paves the way for the broader adoption of Bayes factors in model selection and other quantitative analyses.

The purpose of this research is to tackle the challenge of understanding why certain machine learning models produce incorrect outputs. To achieve this, we need to analyze features from intermediate neural network layers to pinpoint the source of the issue. However, due to the complexity of neural networks and the abundance of computed features, it is extremely difficult for humans to interpret the results correctly. As a result, we cannot trust the results obtained from feature importance tools or visualization techniques. To address this problem, we need to develop a method that is both accurate and reliable. The proposed framework, which we call DiscSense, focuses on elucidating the complexities of neural networks through symbolic transformations. In addition, to ensure the accuracy of the results, we implemented a technique that prevents the introduction of new errors. The results obtained from DiscSense were compared to those from other machine learning models, and the findings revealed that DiscSense yields more plausible explanations. Furthermore, the experiments conducted on various datasets demonstrated that the explanations provided by DiscSense are more likely to be correct when evaluated by multiple criteria. As for the scalability issue, the features of the neural network were significantly reduced, which indicates that the degree of model complexity is not a limitation. As a consequence, we believe that the proposed framework offers a reliable solution for the trustworthy validation of machine learning models.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under elevated temperatures, focusing on spin dynamics and optical transitions. By developing a thermal bath phenmenon model that accounts for spin decoherence, we were able to measure the coherence loss due to lattice vibrations at temperatures up to 500 K. Our research also explored the thermal effects on optical transitions between the ground state and various excited levels of the NV center. To accurately model these interactions, we reconsidered the commonly used (3A2,1A2) transition energy, finding it to be temperature dependent rather than zero at room temperature. Our findings have implications for using NV centers in temperature measurements and offer insights into their optical properties across a broad thermal range.

The underlying mechanisms of local oversight within neural networks, enabling them to be both stable and capable of complex tasks such as pattern recognition and learning, are not yet fully understood. The inhibitory feedback mechanisms present in cortical microcircuits, specifically those involving axons that target dendrites (axodendritic feedback), have long been recognized for their critical role in the proper functioning of these networks. However, the intricate processes occurring within the dendrites of pyramidal cells, the core components of these networks, remain poorly mapped. Our research proposes a novel neural theory that provides a detailed explanation for the computational capabilities of these cells, based on the interaction between different types of neurons within the network. According to this theory, the complex calcium dynamics observed within these cells can be simplified into a single, overstable equilibrium point. This equilibrium is maintained by a self-sustaining oscillatory mechanism involving two types of neurons with distinct firing patterns. Furthermore, our model predicts that the critical aspect of axodendritic feedback is the creation of delayed, self-carried signals, allowing the cell to regulate its own activity through a negative feedback loop. This theory is supported by empirical evidence from various fields, including the study of gene regulation, and provides a foundation for the computational properties that underlie the stability and performance of neural networks based on cortical microcircuits.

A tripodal model is presented that represents spin-1/2 particles on a triangular lattice, with competing isotropic Heisenberg interactions. This model is utilized to investigate the conditions required for quantum ground states with antiferromagnetic N\'{e}el or $\root 3 \of 2$-uplying order. A thorough $\sigma$-model expansion is employed to examine these quantum states near magnetically unstable points within the N\'{e}el or $\root 3 \of 2$-upling phases. The resulting effective actions make visible the marginally unstable modes responsible for these quantum states and reveal the minimal requirements for these states, specifically the accumulation of density of flat bands at the relevant point. The tripodal model represents a specific example of this principle in action. Furthermore, the $\sigma$-model is utilized to derive a more general criterion for the stability of flat-band states within a given magnetic phase. The tripodal model provides an experimental realization of these theories using $SU(3)$ quantum spin systems with large classical counterparts, which are expected to exhibit similar magnetic phases. The associated phase diagrams have been extensively studied through Monte Carlo simulations, showing good agreement with the theoretical predictions.

In this study, a novel method has been introduced by combining B-spline techniques with the self-consistent field method, specifically for solving the Hartree-Fock equation with random central potentials. This approach uses a numerical potential smoothing process to tackle the challenges posed by finite precision calculations and the complexity of atomic systems with high Z values. The method has been successfully applied to a wide range of scenarios, including single atoms with random potentials, atomic chains, electron fluids, and atomic clusters at various levels of electron occupation. The introduced method provides a significant advantage in terms of computational efficiency, with a $10^3$ to $10^6$ times improvement depending on the system in question. This has also enabled the exploration of previously unexamined systems and properties.

The concept of synchronization among oscillators across various fields has been extensively studied, with multiple methods employed to achieve it. In contrast, the phenomenon of synchronization accompanying catastrophic events, known as explosive synchronization, remains an unresolved issue in the study of complex systems. Our research indicates that oscillators within a crowd, regardless of their individual characteristics, can still exhibit a universal universal standard when it comes to the exponential decrease of time it takes to fully synchronize following a sudden disruption. This universal standard is determined by the population's density and a specific measure that takes into account how the oscillators are connected.

We investigate a particular class of matrix factorization problems that involve decomposing a given matrix into the product of several specific matrix factors, such as low-rank matrices, positive semi-definite matrices, and matrices with orthogonal columns and rows. This research is initiated by observing that numerous applications, such as signal processing, statistics, and machine learning, can be viewed through the lens of matrix factorization problems. To facilitate the application of optimization techniques, including those with data augmentation and penalization, we study the geometric properties of a specific objective function that defines these matrix factorization problems. Specifically, we examine the convexity of a particular objective function when subjected to specific matrix decomposition constraints and investigate whether it is over-determined. Our analysis reveals that over-determination is equivalent to analyzing the geometric property of having more constraints than degrees of freedom, and it can be determined by calculating the smallest and largest singular value of a matrix that is derived from the Jacobian matrix of the factorization constraints. We are able to provide a theoretical analysis of the geometric property of matrix factorization problems with specific matrix decomposition constraints, such as low-rank matrices, positive semi-definite matrices, and matrices with orthogonal columns and rows. However, the question of whether these results extend to other fixed-rank matrix optimization problems remains unanswerable with our current methods. In addition, we present an analytical method for determining the geodesic convexity of a particular objective function that defines matrix factorization problems, and we apply this result to

A significant achievement in graph theory related to edge coloring, known as the Four Color Theorem, guarantees that every planar graph can be colored using four colors. This concept has been expanded through the Edge-Two-Coloring conjecture, which asserts that every planar tripartite graph can be edge-colored using two colors. In 2017, a counterexample to this conjecture was proposed by Koch, but it had an issue with local stability. Researchers then made progress in resolving the conjecture by demonstrating that a larger, stable version of Koch's graph required more than two colors. This paper presents the outcome of further analysis on a specific part of Koch's graph, called the "cubic prism." After modifying it to make sure no monochromatic triangles exist, the paper shows that the edge-colored "robust cubic prism" cannot be constructed from a specific set of triangles with a particular connection structure. This discovery implies that the edge-colored "robust cubic prism" requires at least three colors.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

We're proposing a simple, high-energy theory that could have far-reaching implications for various fields, including particle physics, gravitational physics, and cosmology. This idea suggests the existence of extremely heavy, unstable particles whose short lifetimes could result in significantly long-lived 'cosmic threads,' made up of gamma rays, neutrinos, or even other particles. These threads would be produced in vast numbers and extend vast distances, potentially connecting multiple high-energy events together. Our theory aims to provide a comprehensive explanation for several observed phenomena, including large-scale structure formation, the composition of cosmic rays, and the absence of certain particles in high-energy events. To test this theory, we would need extremely large and sensitive detectors capable of observing these cosmic threads, particularly in contexts such as particle collisions at high energies or the decay of heavy particles in deep-inelastic scattering processes.

Our study investigates how a swimming body with viscoelastic properties and asymmetrical front and rear sections moves in a fluid. We used mathematical modeling to analyze a swimmer with a helical trajectory and found that viscoelasticity has contrasting effects on the swimmer's speed depending on the asymmetry of its front and rear sections. When the swimmer's body is symmetrical, viscoelasticity always slows it down. However, when it is asymmetrical, viscoelasticity can speed it up or slow it down, essentially reversing its effect on the swimmer's speed due to its unique shape. We discovered that this opposing effect is caused by how the swimmer's body resists changes in its shape, particularly its ability to store and release energy. This finding suggests that swimmer bodies with viscoelastic properties and asymmetrical front and rear sections could potentially move faster in a fluid than non-viscoelastic swimmers with the same total mass.

We investigated how self-replicating automata in the context of the Cournot game interact and adapt through a process of mutual influence, leading to the emergence of stable coexistence patterns. Our research revealed that coevolutionary genetic algorithms can facilitate the establishment of Nash Equilibrium within a specific range of parameter values. Our findings demonstrate that the interaction between automata's learning mechanisms and their environmental context influences the development of population behavior. Furthermore, we observed that the geometric distribution of automaton positions affects the efficiency of population adaptation. Our study's outcomes also indicate that the complexity of the search space correlates with the efficacy of convergence.

The increasing volume of available textual information necessitates more efficient methods for updating and completing ontologies based on this text. Current approaches to ontology enrichment using machine learning and deep learning have several limitations, including the need for a pre-existing query system to gather relevant data and a lack of consideration for the semantic structure of ontologies. To address these challenges, we present a novel deep learning framework for automatically updating and completing taxonomic and ontological structures from unorganized text. This model utilizes a feature extraction technique called BERT and a graph-based matching method called Graph Attention Network to rank candidate entities for inclusion in the ontology. Our results show that this framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods for entity ranking and achieves promising but less impressive performance for ontology MRR.

A new approach to studying equilibrium conductive behavior through a nonequilibrium setup has been presented. This approach is illustrated using the Ising-doped voter model on a fully connected graph. By analyzing the impact of driving forces on conduct, this approach demonstrates a clear distinction between nonequilibrium steady-state states that are accessible from equilibrium steady-state states. Additionally, this approach reveals that conduct is maximized when the system's stationary distribution is uniform, without relying on specific details of the system's microstructure. Furthermore, this approach enables the examination of conduct in systems that do not have accessible equilibrium steady-state states.

The rapid dissemination of viruses through aerosolized paths presents significant challenges in containing the spread of infectious diseases. Understanding the behavior of aerosols under different meteorological conditions is crucial to comprehending this dissemination. This study leverages numerical modeling to examine the movement of aerosols, assuming they carry a contagious virus, in various atmospheric circumstances, including warm and humid air, freezing temperatures with light ice accumulation, and extreme cold with heavy ice accumulation. A dimensionless group, derived from air density and surface temperature, is found to significantly influence aerosol dynamics, sedimentation, and freezing-related breakdown. Furthermore, modeling reveals that both the Rayleigh dispersion parameter and wind speed substantially impact the dispersal of aerosols, with wind speed exhibiting a more pronounced effect in low-density atmospheres. Additionally, the presence of wind is found to make the coagulation of aerosols more intense, with a greater magnitude in low-density atmospheres. Modeling the behavior of viruses within aerosols considers both direct transmission and transmission resulting from the breakdown of aerosols, with the latter being influenced by the parameters mentioned above, leading to a conclusion that containing the spread of the virus requires a much larger area than would be inferred from modeling that neglects these factors.

The uncertainty quantification in the outputs of machine learning models has been widely recognized and employs various methods to compute confidence levels, including different techniques such as Bayesian neural networks, Monte Carlo dropout, and ensemble-based approaches. Despite significant research in this area, essential problems in quantifying uncertainty remain unresolved for several applications, including classifications with imbalanced data sets and regression tasks. In an effort to accelerate the development of more sophisticated and practical methods for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning models, a standardized framework for measuring uncertainty has been proposed. This framework, referred to as the Ambiguity Measurement Framework (AMF), defines ambiguity as the difference between the predicted output and the actual output and evaluates machine learning models using a variety of data sets. Furthermore, AMF has been enhanced to account for scaling issues by introducing a normalized ambiguity measurement, referred to as the NAMF framework. The performance of different methods for quantifying uncertainty, including different loss functions and differentially weighted ensembles, is examined and compared to the proposed AMF standard. The results of these experiments demonstrate the superiority of certain methods for quantifying uncertainty and suggest areas for improvement in machine learning models. In addition, the impact of model complexity and the number of network parameters on the performance of models for quantifying uncertainty has been investigated. The results of these experiments have been presented in the form of animations and a supplementary video.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish connections between the polynomial ring's parameter, specifically its general and symbolic powers, and specific properties of $\mathcal{D}$, including its components' inclusions, the dimension of its underlying undirected version, and the number of its directed edges. Furthermore, conditions are identified under which the canonical module of $I(\mathcal{D})$ is generated by the edge ideal's pure powers, effectively extending a notable result from undirected graphs to directed graphs.

We've obtained an explicit, semi-analytic expression for the partition function of a Hermitian $O(N)$ symmetric quadratic matrix model in the finite $N$ case. This involves combining an orthogonal polynomial approach with a bosonic TMTB type supermatrix model, allowing us to extend previous findings related to the partition function's symmetry under the $O(N)$ group and calculate correlation functions of the matrix model.

Deep Learning systems like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are integral to various security applications with Deep Learning (DL). These CNN models rely on floating-point arithmetic, which makes them prone to hardware-induced errors, specifically those caused by finite precision in hardware. Such vulnerabilities could be exploited to manipulate the outcomes of these models through techniques like precision manipulation attacks. To counter this risk, we employ activation range monitoring, a novel approach that determines accuracy based on the range of activation values rather than comparison with expected output. This approach is effective against malicious attackers seeking to manipulate the models' behavior and has the added benefit of enhancing the robustness of the models in the face of hardware-induced errors due to the use of a non-zero epsilon in relevance feedback. Our research demonstrates that using activation range monitoring, DL systems like CNN can maintain a certain level of accuracy even in the presence of hardware-induced errors and malicious attacks, thereby achieving a level of resilience and security.

The method we propose can calculate the amount of money that each company must pay as settlement in a scenario where the total amount owed is shared among them based on their respective shares of earned commissions. This method is put into practice through an algorithm developed for the Romanian Ministry of Finance in its dealings with large firms like Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Apple.

This study establishes a one-parameter collection of solutions for the Yang-Baxter equation using the Jordanian twist. The convention used yields a two-component matrix product, and specific parameter settings are identified that reproduce well-known formulas, including the 9-vertex and alternating sign solutions. The method employed involves a novel expansion technique for the Jordanian twist, resulting in a twisted $R$-matrix expressed as a sum of two matrix products. The 6-vertex solution is also generated with this approach, and further analysis reveals that the 8-vertex solution can be expressed as a local limit of the 9-vertex solution, a relationship that cannot be captured using the conventional expansion method.

Cross-lingual studies have made significant progress in recent years, thanks to advances in word representations and embeddings. Current embeddings, such as word2vec and bilingual word embeddings, have demonstrated success in multiple languages by capturing the grammatical and semantic nuances of languages. However, these embeddings have several limitations, notably that they are not easily interpretable, cannot be directly related to each other, and do not preserve the semantic relationships between words. To address these challenges, our research introduces a novel, multi-lingual shared semantic framework based on graph embeddings. This framework utilizes a non-overlapping set of words to define a graph for each language and extracts the underlying latent factors to create a shared multi-lingual embedding space. To prevent linguistic isolation, our research proposes clustering translation pairs and merging the graphs based on the obtained clusters, resulting in a single, unified multi-lingual embedding space. This space is demonstrated to improve semantic retention and preserve semantic relationships across languages through extensive experiments.

This study reports the production rates of pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons in 13.6 TeV Xe-Xe collisions, based on data from the ALICE detector at the LHC. A detailed analysis of midrapidity particle spectra was performed for central collisions at 5.44 TeV, obtained through interpolation of lower-energy data. The resulting particle densities are compared with the GLV string-melting model and the TRENTO model, a subset of the EPOS LHC model, to gain insight into the initial conditions of these collisions.

The task of conversational state tracking (CST) is crucial in automated dialogue systems, as it enables the systems to respond effectively. CST is an ongoing challenge due to the inherent uncertainty associated with annotation data. The problem is compounded by the fact that current methods overlook the consideration of label uncertainty, which is a significant shortcoming. To address this shortcoming, we present a new uncertainty-aware approach for CST, which employs a unique combination of both segmentation-based and state-based uncertainty estimation techniques. Our approach is designed to be robust to label uncertainty and is validated through a series of experiments conducted on the DSTC9 Task 2 data. The results show a notable improvement of 8.51% in the overall joint goal accuracy when compared to the baseline models that disregard label uncertainty.

This study aims to offer a mathematical framework modeling the spread of information that sparked the Chilean protests in 2019, focusing on an approach that doesn't consider global connectivity. The model, consisting of ordinary and partial differential equations, seeks to depict the outbreak of protests as information spreads through interconnected regions in Chile. The model's equations are solved to simulate the protests using the method of approximation, and results are validated with actual event data, showing a plausible correlation. The simulation reveals how the model's parameters influence protest intensity in different regions, raising implications for epidemiological models that incorporate social unrest as a co-occurring phenomenon.

Determining Star Formation Rates (SFRs) is fundamental in understanding the behavior of galaxies throughout the history of the universe. While using rest-frame far-infrared and submillimeter light to estimate SFRs is relatively straightforward and accurate, using optical line diagnostics is a more common method, although it relies on line emission being a true indicator of dust-observed star formation. Recently, the use of optical recombination lines, which are closely linked to line diagnostics, has been proposed as a novel SFR indicator. This study utilizes a sample of 111 galaxies at redshifts 0.5-2.5 to compare three different methods of calculating their SFRs: based on ${\rm H}\alpha$ and ${\rm H}\beta$ line fluxes, line diagnostics in general, and Structural Reconstruction of Line Emission with Physical Parameters (SED-fitting). The research reveals that the ${\rm H}\alpha$-based method generally overestimates the SFRs by around 2.5 times the true values, while line diagnostics can recover the actual SFRs up to 90% accurately. The study also shows that using optical recombination lines over estimates the gas-phase line diagnostics-based SFR by around 2.5 times, which is comparable to the results from the ${\rm H}\alpha$-based method. The study indicates the need for a correction factor for optical recombination lines at high redshifts to obtain accurate SFR

We're investigating the capabilities of functions within polynomial form that, when squared, yield non-negative outcomes, including those on the perimeter of this realm. This analysis focuses on linear combinations of parabolas and examines how sums of these parabolas behave under translations. It demonstrates that the extreme values of this combination can be made arbitrarily close to certain curved shapes by moving it through a series of translations. It also shows that some of these curved shapes cannot be expressed as the combination of two parabolas, even if those parabolas are allowed to be negative. It further reveals that all rational functions with non-negative integer exponents within a specific range can be seen as the combination of a finite number of parabolas, although some of these combinations will be non-positive for certain values. It demonstrates that the ability to express a specific shape as the combination of two parabolas is a local property, as is the ability to express a specific function as the combination of two non-negative polynomials. It also presents an infinite number of linear functions that cannot be expressed as the combination of two non-negative polynomials, as well as an infinite number of polynomials with non-negative coefficients that cannot be expressed as the combination of two non-negative polynomials. It demonstrates that all functions within a specific range can be seen as the combination of a finite number of polynomials with non-negative coefficients, although some of these combinations will be non-positive for certain values. We re-examine how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about unitarity. We pay particular attention to the part governing neutrino-lepton scattering and gather constraints from experiment and theoretical limits on its magnitude.
